ScaffoldAgent: Utility-Guided Dynamic Outline Optimization for Open-Ended Deep Research

Abstract

Open-ended deep research (OEDR) requires systems to acquire knowledge through multi-round retrieval and generate coherent long-form reports. The outline plays a central role as a structural scaffold that coordinates retrieval, evidence organization, and generation. However, existing methods either fix the outline before writing or refine it with local heuristics, leading to scaffold drift under continuous information accumulation and delayed feedback for evaluating outline modifications. We propose ScaffoldAgent, a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for OEDR. ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three operations: Expansion, Contraction, and Revision, enabling controlled updates to the report scaffold. It further introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that estimates the downstream value of each outline operation from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. The resulting utility signal guides node selection, operation scheduling, and termination during inference. Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show that ScaffoldAgent consistently improves long-form report generation and factual grounding over existing deep research agents.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a key foundation for building increasingly capable language agents Bubeck et al. (2023). Recent advances in reasoning-oriented models, such as DeepSeek-R1 Shao et al. (2024b) and the OpenAI o-series Jaech et al. (2024), have substantially improved LLM performance on structured tasks, including mathematical reasoning and complex question answering Trinh et al. (2024). Beyond single-turn generation, tool-augmented LLMs, i.e., Agents Li et al. (2026), can now interact with external environments and perform iterative planning, searching and self-correction Jiang et al. (2024); Yao et al. (2022a); Zhang et al. (2026); Shinn et al. (2024); Schick et al. (2023).

This agentic paradigm has shown strong potential in software engineering Jimenez et al. (2024) and open-world web navigation Zhou et al. (2024); Mialon et al. (2024). However, open-ended tasks that require agents to acquire knowledge through multi-round retrieval and synthesize accumulated evidence into coherent long-form reports still remain challenging. These tasks, recently studied under formulation of Open-ended Deep Research (OEDR) Li et al. (2025); Du et al. (2025), require not only effective information seeking and content generation, but persistent content organization over evolving evidence.

Unlike task-oriented agents that execute a fixed plan toward a well-defined goal Jimenez et al. (2024); Mialon et al. (2024), OEDR is organized around an open-ended objective whose scope evolves as new evidence is discovered. In each round, the system must retrieve new information, reconcile it with prior reasoning, and update the organization of the emerging report Li et al. (2025); Li et al. (2026); Prabhakar et al. (2025). Within this loop, the outline is not merely a pre-writing plan, but an active structural scaffold: it guides what to search, indexes evidence under appropriate sections, and constrains final report generation Shao et al. (2024a); Xiong et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025).

However, existing deep research systems still face substantial limitations: As report grows in length and topical breadth, a static or poorly maintained outline may gradually drift from the evolving evidence space, leading to redundant coverage, missing perspectives, or incoherent section organization. One line of work follows a plan-then-write paradigm, where the outline is fixed before report generation begins Shao et al. (2024a); Lee et al. (2025); Han et al. (2025), causing the planned outline to diverge from the evolving information space Xiong et al. (2025) gradually. Another line of work introduces dynamic outline update mechanisms but predominantly relies on heuristic rules or local feedback Wang et al. (2025); Shi et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025); Wan et al. (2025), lack a unified optimization objective that jointly accounts for retrieval quality, structural soundness, and generation quality Wu et al. (2025); Xiong et al. (2025): for instance, update outline based solely on newly retrieved documents  Li et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025), or signals that do not propagate beyond current step Wan et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025).

This limitation gives rise to two core challenges, as illustrated in Figure 1. First, without explicit control over structural evolution, iterative refinement may cause scaffold drift: newly retrieved evidence can trigger redundant branches, uneven topic granularity, or misplaced subtopics, progressively destabilizing the global hierarchy of the outline (C1). Second, the usefulness of an outline modification is difficult to determine at the moment it is made. Any section modification may only reveal its value after subsequent retrieval and trial generation, leading to delayed feedback to evaluate the downstream utility (C2).

To address these challenges, we propose ScaffoldAgent, a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for open-ended deep research. Rather than treating the outline as a fixed pre-writing plan, ScaffoldAgent maintains it as an evolving structural scaffold that coordinates retrieval, evidence organization, and report generation throughout the research process. To mitigate C1, ScaffoldAgent formulates outline evolution as a structured decision process with three explicit operations: Expansion, Contraction, and Revision. Inspired by classical belief revision theory Alchourrón et al. (1985), these operations allow the system to incorporate new information, merge redundant branches, and revise weakly supported sections while preserving hierarchical consistency. To address C2, ScaffoldAgent introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that estimates the usefulness of each outline modification from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. A Reporter Agent performs trial writing under the current outline, and its generation quality and citation grounding provide downstream feedback. The resulting utility estimate serves as an inference-time control signal for node selection, operation scheduling, and termination, enabling ScaffoldAgent to optimize outline evolution beyond local heuristic refinement. Contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose ScaffoldAgent, a utility-guided framework that treats the outline as an evolving structural scaffold and optimizes it through explicit operations, including Expansion, Contraction, and Revision.

  • •

    We introduce a utility-guided feedback mechanism that evaluates outline operations from retrieval, structure, and generation, enabling inference-time control over node selection, operation scheduling, and termination.

  • •

    Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show that ScaffoldAgent consistently outperforms existing deep research agents, validating the effectiveness of utility-guided outline optimization for improving long-form report generation and factual grounding.

2 Related Work

2.1 Open-Ended Deep Research

Open-Ended Deep Research (OEDR) extends bounded question answering to long-horizon evidence collection and grounded report synthesis, as formalized by recent benchmarks Du et al. (2025); Coelho et al. (2025). Built upon tool-augmented agents and search-augmented reasoning  Yao et al. (2022b); Trivedi et al. (2023); Jin et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026), existing OEDR systems have explored several complementary directions. STORM and TTD-DR follow plan- or refinement-oriented workflows for long-form research report generation Shao et al. (2024a); Han et al. (2025). WebWeaver and AgentCPM-Report further introduce dynamic outlines to connect evidence acquisition with report writing, either through planner-writer collaboration or drafting-driven deepening Li et al. (2025); Li et al. (2026). EDR, RhinoInsight, and FS-Researcher enhance OEDR from the perspectives of multi-agent coordination, behavior/context control, and persistent external memory Prabhakar et al. (2025); Lei et al. (2025); Zhu et al. (2026). While these methods improve retrieval, memory, agent coordination, or writing feedback, outline updates are still largely driven by fixed workflows, local heuristics, or single-stage feedback. They do not unify retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality into a single utility signal for node selection, operation scheduling, and termination.

2.2 Report Generation

Grounded report generation builds on retrieval-augmented and attributed generation, where external evidence improves factuality and supports citation-aware writing Lewis et al. (2021); Menick et al. (2022); Gao et al. (2023). For long-form report generation, a common solution is the plan-then-write paradigm, which first constructs an outline or high-level report plan and then generates content section by section to maintain global organization Yao et al. (2019); Yang et al. (2023); Yang et al. (2022); Bai et al. (2025); Wan et al. (2025). More adaptive methods further update outlines, memory, or task graphs during extended generation: DOME uses dynamic hierarchical outlines with memory enhancement, WriteHERE performs heterogeneous recursive planning, and survey-generation systems such as SurveyGen-I and SciSage use evolving plans, memory-guided writing, or reflection to improve cross-section coherence, coverage, and citation quality Wang et al. (2025); Xiong et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025); Shi et al. (2025). These methods improve the structure and revision of long reports, but mainly optimize the generated text or local writing plan.

3 OEDR Task Formulation

Given a research question qq and access to a large-scale document collection 𝒟\mathcal{D}, Open-ended Deep Research (OEDR) aims to generate a structurally coherent and well-cited long-form report. Different from one-shot retrieval-augmented generation, OEDR requires a system to iteratively search for evidence, organize the acquired information, and synthesize the final report.

We view OEDR as a dynamic interaction among three components: Search, Outline, and Report. Search retrieves external evidence from the document collection; Outline organizes the accumulated evidence into a hierarchical scaffold that defines the scope and structure of the report; and Report transforms the organized evidence into coherent long-form text. These components are mutually dependent: the outline determines what should be searched next, newly retrieved evidence may reshape the outline, and report generation can expose missing support or structural gaps that require further refinement.

4 Method

4.1 ScaffoldAgent Overview

ScaffoldAgent instantiates OEDR as a utility-guided outline optimization process. Starting from a root outline node initialized by the input question, ScaffoldAgent iteratively grows and refines an outline tree until it becomes a stable scaffold for long-form report generation. At iteration tt, we denote the current outline tree as

𝒯t=(𝒱t,𝒫t,Φt),\mathcal{T}_{t}=(\mathcal{V}_{t},\mathcal{P}_{t},\Phi_{t}), (1)

where 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} is the set of outline nodes, 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} denotes parent–child relations, and Φt\Phi_{t} stores node-level attributes. Each node v∈𝒱tv\in\mathcal{V}_{t} corresponds to a section or subsection and is associated with

Φt​(v)=(hv,ℰv,θv),\Phi_{t}(v)=\big(h_{v},\mathcal{E}_{v},\theta_{v}\big), (2)

where hvh_{v} is the node intent, ℰv\mathcal{E}_{v} is the supporting evidence and report-chunk attached to this node, and θv\theta_{v} records historical utility statistics. The initial tree contains only the root node derived from the input question 𝒯0=Init⁡(q).\mathcal{T}_{0}=\mathrm{Init}(q).

ScaffoldAgent consists of three specialized agents. The Outline Agent serves as the central controller: it maintains the evolving outline tree, selects which node to visit, and decides how the selected node should be updated. The Search Agent retrieves external evidence when an update requires new information. The Reporter Agent performs trial writing during optimization and produces the final report after the outline converges.

The overall process is node-centric. At each iteration, the Outline Agent first selects a target node vtv_{t} according to utility feedback, and then chooses one structural operation oto_{t} from:

ot∈{Expansion,Contraction,Revision}.o_{t}\in\{\text{Expansion},\text{Contraction},\text{Revision}\}. (3)

The selected operation updates the outline tree and produces new utility feedback:

𝒯t+1,Ut=Update⁡(𝒯t,vt,ot,πres,πrep),\mathcal{T}_{t+1},U_{t}=\mathrm{Update}\big(\mathcal{T}_{t},v_{t},o_{t};\pi_{\text{res}},\pi_{\text{rep}}\big), (4)

where πres\pi_{\text{res}} and πrep\pi_{\text{rep}} denote the Search Agent and Reporter Agent, respectively. Expansion and Revision invoke both the Search Agent and the Reporter Agent, since they require additional evidence and downstream writing feedback. Contraction reorganizes existing evidence and therefore only invokes the Reporter Agent to evaluate whether the compressed local structure remains coherent and grounded. The resulting utility feedback updates node statistics and guides the next iteration. When further refinement brings limited utility gain, ScaffoldAgent stops optimizing the outline and generates the final report along the converged scaffold.

4.2 Evolving Outline Tree

The outline tree is the central state of ScaffoldAgent. It starts from a root node derived from the input question and gradually evolves into a hierarchical report scaffold. Each node represents a potential section or subsection, with an intent description that specifies what the section should cover, a set of supporting evidence, and utility statistics accumulated from previous visits. By attaching evidence directly to outline nodes, ScaffoldAgent uses the outline not only as a writing plan, but also as an evidence index that connects retrieval and generation.

At each iteration, the Outline Agent must decide which node should be visited next. A useful selection strategy should revisit low-quality nodes that require correction, while still exploring under-visited parts of the tree to avoid early local bias. For each node vv, ScaffoldAgent maintains utility statistics

θv=(nv,u¯​(v)),\theta_{v}=(n_{v},\bar{u}(v)), (5)

where nvn_{v} is the number of visits and u¯​(v)\bar{u}(v) is the running mean utility of previous actions applied to this node. Let 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} denote the set of outline nodes at iteration tt. The next target node is selected using a UCB-style rule:

vt=arg⁡maxv∈𝒱t⁡(−u¯​(v)+c​ln⁡Ntnv),v_{t}=\arg\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{t}}\left(-\bar{u}(v)+c\sqrt{\frac{\ln N_{t}}{n_{v}}}\right), (6)

where Nt=∑v∈𝒱tnvN_{t}=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{t}}n_{v} is the total visit count and cc is the exploration coefficient. The first term prioritizes low-utility nodes that need improvement, while the second term encourages exploration of rarely visited nodes.

After an operation is applied to the selected node, its statistics are updated with the newly obtained utility UtU_{t}:

nvt←nvt+1,u¯​(vt)←u¯​(vt)+Ut−u¯​(vt)nvt.n_{v_{t}}\leftarrow n_{v_{t}}+1,\bar{u}(v_{t})\leftarrow\bar{u}(v_{t})+\frac{U_{t}-\bar{u}(v_{t})}{n_{v_{t}}}. (7)

This update allows the system to accumulate evidence about which parts of the outline remain weak and which parts have already become stable.

After a target node is selected, the Outline Agent determines how to update it according to its utility profile. A node with insufficient topical granularity tends to trigger Expansion; redundant or overlapping sibling nodes tend to trigger Contraction; and a weakly supported or outdated node tends to trigger Revision. The outline tree keeps evolving until the marginal utility gain becomes small:

1k​∑i=t−k+1tΔ​Ui<ϵ,Δ​Ui=Ui−Ui−1.\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=t-k+1}^{t}\Delta U_{i}<\epsilon,\Delta U_{i}=U_{i}-U_{i-1}. (8)

This indicates that further structural changes are unlikely to improve the final report. At this point, the Reporter Agent generates the final report along the converged outline.

4.3 Outline Agent’s Actions

To mitigate scaffold drift (C1), ScaffoldAgent updates the outline through three explicit operations: Expansion, Contraction, and Revision. These operations are inspired by belief revision theory Alchourrón et al. (1985), but are used here as practical structural actions rather than formal logical operators. They correspond to three common outline deficiencies: insufficient granularity, redundant branching, and weak evidential grounding.

  • •

    Expansion. Expansion is used when the selected node is too broad to support focused retrieval or detailed writing. The Outline Agent decomposes the node into several finer-grained child nodes, each with a clearer intent. Since newly created subtopics require supporting evidence, Expansion first invokes the Search Agent to retrieve documents for the child nodes. The Reporter Agent then performs trial writing on the expanded subtree to evaluate whether the new structure improves downstream report generation.

  • •

    Contraction. Contraction is used when sibling nodes are semantically overlapping, overly fragmented, or repeatedly supported by similar evidence. The Outline Agent merges redundant branches into representative nodes and regenerates their intents to cover the merged content. Since Contraction reorganizes existing evidence rather than introducing new subtopics, it does not invoke the Search Agent. The Reporter Agent is used to check whether the compressed local structure remains coherent, non-redundant, and sufficiently grounded.

  • •

    Revision. Revision is used when the selected node is weakly supported, outdated, or misaligned with its accumulated evidence. The Outline Agent preserves the node’s position in the global tree but refreshes its intent and evidence grounding. Revision invokes the Search Agent to retrieve additional evidence for the node, and then invokes the Reporter Agent to assess whether the revised node better supports grounded writing. Unlike Expansion, Revision does not increase the size of the tree.

These three operations define how the outline tree evolves during research. Expansion increases topical granularity, Contraction controls redundancy, and Revision improves local evidence grounding. Together, they allow ScaffoldAgent to maintain a scaffold that is stable enough for coherent writing while remaining adaptive to newly acquired evidence.

4.4 Utility-Guided Feedback

To address delayed feedback (C2), ScaffoldAgent uses utility as an inference-time control signal rather than a gradient-based training objective. After each node-level operation, the system evaluates the updated local scaffold from three perspectives: whether it acquires useful evidence, whether it improves structural organization, and whether it supports grounded writing. We denote the overall utility at iteration tt as:

Ut=λ1​Uret+λ2​Ustr+λ3​Ugen,U_{t}=\lambda_{1}U_{\text{ret}}+\lambda_{2}U_{\text{str}}+\lambda_{3}U_{\text{gen}}, (9)

where UretU_{\text{ret}}, UstrU_{\text{str}}, and UgenU_{\text{gen}} are retrieval, structure, and generation utility, respectively. The coefficients λ1\lambda_{1}, λ2\lambda_{2}, and λ3\lambda_{3} control their relative importance.

  • •

    Retrieval Utility. UretU_{\text{ret}} evaluates whether newly acquired evidence is both relevant to the target node and non-redundant with existing evidence:

    Uret=wrel​Rel+wnov​Nov.U_{\text{ret}}=w_{\text{rel}}\mathrm{Rel}+w_{\text{nov}}\mathrm{Nov}. (10)

    Here, Rel\mathrm{Rel} measures semantic relevance between retrieved documents and the target node intent, while Nov\mathrm{Nov} measures novelty relative to evidence already attached to the outline tree.

  • •

    Structure Utility. UstrU_{\text{str}} evaluates whether the outline scaffold remains coherent, balanced, and non-redundant:

    Ustr=wcoh​Coh+wbal​Bal−wred​Red.U_{\text{str}}=w_{\text{coh}}\mathrm{Coh}+w_{\text{bal}}\mathrm{Bal}-w_{\text{red}}\mathrm{Red}. (11)

    Here, Coh\mathrm{Coh} captures semantic consistency among related nodes, Bal\mathrm{Bal} measures structural balance, and Red\mathrm{Red} penalizes redundant sibling branches.

  • •

    Generation Utility. UgenU_{\text{gen}} evaluates whether the current scaffold can support grounded writing. The Reporter Agent performs trial writing on the affected node or subtree, and the generated text is scored by:

    Ugen=α​ρsup+β​ρcov−γ​ρred,U_{\text{gen}}=\alpha\rho_{\text{sup}}+\beta\rho_{\text{cov}}-\gamma\rho_{\text{red}}, (12)

    where ρsup\rho_{\text{sup}} measures citation support, ρcov\rho_{\text{cov}} measures alignment between node intent and generated content, and ρred\rho_{\text{red}} penalizes cross-section redundancy.

5 Experiments

We evaluate ScaffoldAgent against the following research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: Does ScaffoldAgent outperform existing methods in open-ended deep research?

  • •

    RQ2: How much does each internal component of ScaffoldAgent—the three outline actions (Expansion, Contraction, Revision) and the three utility dimensions (UretU_{\text{ret}}, UstrU_{\text{str}}, UgenU_{\text{gen}}) that score them contribute to the final performance?

  • •

    RQ3: Can ScaffoldAgent handle multi-turn follow-ups by incrementally updating a previously built outline tree?

5.1 Experimental Setup

❶ Evaluation Benchmarks. We evaluate ScaffoldAgent on two open-ended deep-research benchmarks: DeepResearch Bench Du et al. (2025) and DeepResearch Gym Coelho et al. (2025). The former assesses report quality via RACE (Overall, Comprehensiveness, Insight, Instruction-following, Readability) and factual grounding via FACT (effective citation rate Eff.c. and citation accuracy C.acc.). The latter scores six report dimensions: Clarity, Depth, Balance, Breadth, Supportability, and Insightfulness. Further details are deferred to Appendix B.

❷Baselines. We compare ScaffoldAgent against baselines from three paradigms: Naive (direct Prompt and RAG), Single-Agent (ReAct Yao et al. (2022a), IRCoT Trivedi et al. (2023), WebShaper Tao et al. (2025)), and Multi-Agent (STORM Shao et al. (2024a), WebWeaver Li et al. (2025), EDR Prabhakar et al. (2025), StackPlanner Zhang et al. (2026)). Further details are deferred to Appendix C.

❸Implementation Details. We use DeepSeek-V3.2 Liu et al. (2024) and Qwen3-32B Yang et al. (2025) as backbone LLMs, and adopt Bocha as the web-search API. Further implementation details are deferred to Appendix D.

5.2 Main Result Analysis (RQ1)

We evaluate ScaffoldAgent on DeepResearch Bench (Table 1, both Qwen3-32B Yang et al. (2025) and DeepSeek-V3.2 backbones) and DeepResearch Gym (Table 2, Qwen3-32B).

Comparison with Baselines.

ScaffoldAgent achieves the strongest Qwen3-32B results on DeepResearch Bench, reaching 44.70 RACE Overall and improving over the best baseline, IRCoT, by +2.24+2.24 points. The gain is accompanied by stronger factual grounding: ScaffoldAgent obtains the highest Eff.c. (30.42) and C.acc. (54.32), whereas the strongest single-agent baselines remain substantially lower in citation accuracy (ReAct 23.78 and IRCoT 40.04). Multi-agent baselines do not close this gap: WebWeaver is competitive in RACE Overall (41.28) but trails by 13.42 points in C.acc., while EDR and STORM score below 41 RACE Overall and below 37 C.acc. These results show that ScaffoldAgent improves report quality without sacrificing grounding.

Robustness across Backbones.

On DeepSeek-V3.2, ScaffoldAgent remains the best method in RACE Overall, reaching 48.27 and surpassing StackPlanner by +1.45+1.45 points. It also ranks first on all five RACE sub-dimensions, indicating that the improvement is not driven by a single aspect of report quality. Baseline behavior changes substantially across backbones: IRCoT drops from 42.46 to 39.73 RACE Overall, while StackPlanner rises from 41.55 to 46.82. In contrast, ScaffoldAgentimproves monotonically on every Bench metric (RACE 44.70→\to48.27, Eff.c. 30.42→\to51.18, C.acc. 54.32→\to62.20), suggesting that the utility-guided framework scales with stronger backbone capability rather than overfitting to a particular model.

Multi-Dimensional Evaluation on Gym.

On DeepResearch Gym, ScaffoldAgent achieves the highest average score, 75.83, outperforming the strongest baseline EDR by +1.78+1.78 points. It leads three of the six dimensions, Depth (82.40), Breadth (85.20), and Insight (68.80), which is consistent with its explicit outline expansion and refinement process. Although EDR obtains the highest Supportability score (89.50), ScaffoldAgent remains competitive on Supportability (79.80) and keeps the remaining dimensions close to the best baseline, showing that its gains in depth and insight do not come from degrading overall structural quality.

5.3 Component Analysis

❶ Outline-Action Behavior and Ablation. For RQ2 (action side), Table 3 ablates the three AGM-aligned outline actions. Removing Contraction lets the tree widen unchecked, dropping RACE 48.27→\to44.72 (−3.55-3.55) and C.acc. 62.20→\to57.79. Removing Revision blocks evidence refresh and gives the lowest single-action RACE (43.09, −5.18-5.18); C.acc. slips only to 58.11 because the retrieved evidence still locally supports the (ill-posed) claims it was fetched for citations stay attributable, but the underlying arguments are weaker, which RACE penalizes and FACT does not. Disabling both (Expansion-only) yields suboptimal results across on all three metrics (RACE 41.73, Eff.c. 45.20, C.acc. 59.32), and we further observe non-terminating runs in which the outline keeps inflating until the budget is exhausted, confirming that the two shrinking actions are load-bearing. Figure 3 corroborates this from the behavior side: Expansion dominates the early budget, then Contraction and Revision take over for merging and refresh, with all three active throughout.

❷Utility-Dimension Ablation. For RQ2 (utility side), Table 4 isolates the three utility terms used score candidate actions. Removing UretU_{\text{ret}} mainly weakens evidence supply, sharply reducing Eff.c. 51.18→\to39.42 (−11.76-11.76) while C.acc. drops more mildly 62.20→\to55.68, suggesting that retrieval utility primarily controls whether the tree acquires enough relevant, non-redundant evidence. Removing UstrU_{\text{str}} disrupts global outline organization, dropping RACE 48.27→\to44.17 (−4.10-4.10) with only moderate FACT degradation (Eff.c. 47.86, C.acc. 58.41); local claims may remain attributable, but redundant or unbalanced branches weaken comprehensiveness, insight, and readability. Removing UgenU_{\text{gen}} is mostdamaging overall, yielding the lowest RACE (43.58, −4.69-4.69) and the largest C.acc. drop 62.20→\to50.82 (−11.38-11.38), since trial writing directly scores citation support, intent coverage, and redundancy. Together, these results show that UretU_{\text{ret}} supplies evidence, UstrU_{\text{str}} regularizes the scaffold, and UgenU_{\text{gen}} aligns outline optimization with downstream report generation.

❸Multi-turn Interaction. For RQ3, Table 5 evaluates whether ScaffoldAgent can handle user follow-ups by incrementally updating an existing outline tree. We compare against two ReAct-based baselines (details in Appendix B): ReAct-FW writes a fresh report from a query formed by combining the original query and the follow-up query, while ReAct-GR conditions on the first-turn report and globally rewrites it according to the follow-up query. ReAct-FW can address the new instruction and remains fluent, but discarding the first-turn report leads to severe content loss (Com. 6.60). ReAct-GR preserves more prior content (Com. 10.90), yet rewriting the whole report still causes logical drift (Log. 11.55). In contrast, ScaffoldAgent updates only the subtree affected by the follow-up through localized Revision/Expansion, leaving unrelated sections intact. Such updates yield the best score across dimension and raises the total score to 72.60, suggesting that the AGM decomposition provides a practical mechanism for non-destructive multi-turn refinement.

6 Conclusion

ScaffoldAgent presents a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for open-ended deep research. Instead of treating the outline as a static pre-writing plan, ScaffoldAgent maintains it as an evolving scaffold that coordinates evidence retrieval, content organization, and long-form report generation. By modeling outline evolution through three explicit operations, Expansion, Contraction, and Revision, the framework enables controllable structural updates that incorporate new information, reduce redundant branches, and refresh weakly supported sections. ScaffoldAgent further introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that jointly considers retrieval gain, structural quality, and trial-generation quality, providing inference-time signals for node selection, operation scheduling, and termination. Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show that ScaffoldAgent achieves strong overall performance in report quality and factual grounding compared with existing deep research agents, demonstrating the effectiveness of dynamic outline optimization for open-ended research tasks.

Limitations

Despite the consistent improvements achieved by ScaffoldAgent, several directions remain for future work. First, our multi-turn evaluation is still preliminary. Current open-ended deep research benchmarks are largely single-turn, whereas realistic use often involves longer dialogues in which users iteratively revise the scope, constraints, or subtopics. Future work could develop longer multi-turn trajectories and more comprehensive evaluation protocols for such interactive research scenarios. Second, due to the substantial cost of large-scale deep research evaluation, our experiments are conducted primarily with widely used open-source foundation models and a fixed search interface, rather than the strongest available models and search systems. Future work may further investigate how the framework scales when combined with more capable backbone models, advanced search infrastructures, and larger retrieval budgets. Finally, ScaffoldAgentcurrently relies on utility-based inference-time control without explicitly learning an outline-evolution policy. While this design is lightweight and effective, dynamic outline optimization naturally forms a sequential decision-making problem. A promising direction for future work is to learn such policies with reinforcement learning, potentially improving outline expansion, refinement, and information gathering throughout the report generation process.

Ethical considerations

All experiments in this work were carried out on publicly available open-ended deep research benchmarks, including DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym, following their respective licenses and usage terms. The study does not involve human or animal subjects, and we did not collect, use, or disclose any personally identifiable information.

Appendix A More Method

Optimization Algorithm.

Algorithm 1 summarizes the inference-time outline optimization (Opt.) process of ScaffoldAgent.

Utility Signals and Computation.

We provide further details on how the utility components in Section 4.4 are computed. The overall utility is computed as

Ut=λ1​Uret+λ2​Ustr+λ3​Ugen,U_{t}=\lambda_{1}U_{\text{ret}}+\lambda_{2}U_{\text{str}}+\lambda_{3}U_{\text{gen}}, (13)

where retrieval utility, structure utility, and generation utility capture complementary aspects of the updated local scaffold.

Retrieval utility. After an action retrieves a set of new documents Δ​ℰv={d1,…,dk}\Delta\mathcal{E}_{v}=\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{k}\} for the target node vv, we compute a retrieval reward following the intuition of maximal marginal relevance (MMR)Carbonell and Goldstein (1998): useful evidence should be relevant to the current information need while adding non-redundant information. Formally, we define

Uret=wrel​Rel+wnov​Nov,U_{\text{ret}}=w_{\text{rel}}\mathrm{Rel}+w_{\text{nov}}\mathrm{Nov}, (14)

where wrelw_{\text{rel}} and wnovw_{\text{nov}} control the trade-off between relevance and novelty.

Rel\mathrm{Rel} measures semantic alignment between the retrieved documents and the target node intent. Let qvq_{v} denote the retrieval query derived from node vv, including its title and local outline context. Given the embedding of qvq_{v} and each retrieved document djd_{j}, relevance is computed as

Rel=1k​∑j=1ksim⁡(qv,dj),\mathrm{Rel}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathrm{sim}(q_{v},d_{j}), (15)

where sim⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathrm{sim}(\cdot,\cdot) denotes cosine similarity in the embedding space.

Nov\mathrm{Nov} measures the marginal information gain of the retrieved documents with respect to cached evidence in the current outline. For each new document djd_{j}, we compare it with the existing evidence set ℰcache\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cache}} attached to the target node and related outline nodes:

Nov=1k​∑j=1k(1−maxd′∈ℰcache⁡sim⁡(dj,d′)).\mathrm{Nov}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left(1-\max_{d^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cache}}}\mathrm{sim}(d_{j},d^{\prime})\right). (16)

This term assigns higher scores to documents that introduce information not already covered by the current scaffold, thereby encouraging broader evidence acquisition rather than repeated retrieval of similar passages.

Structure utility. Structure utility evaluates whether the updated outline remains coherent, balanced, and non-redundant:

Ustr=wcoh​Coh+wbal​Bal−wred​Red.U_{\text{str}}=w_{\text{coh}}\mathrm{Coh}+w_{\text{bal}}\mathrm{Bal}-w_{\text{red}}\mathrm{Red}. (17)

Coh\mathrm{Coh} is estimated by an LLM judge that assesses whether the child intents are semantically consistent with the parent intent and whether the subtree forms a coherent decomposition of the target topic.

Bal\mathrm{Bal} measures whether the updated local subtree has an appropriate depth and branching structure. Let 𝒯v\mathcal{T}_{v} denote the subtree rooted at node vv, and let bib_{i} be the number of children of node ii in this subtree. We define

Bal=exp⁡(−Δd−Δb),\mathrm{Bal}=\exp(-\Delta_{d}-\Delta_{b}), (18)

where Δd=|depth⁡(𝒯v)−d⋆|/d⋆\Delta_{d}=|\mathrm{depth}(\mathcal{T}_{v})-d^{\star}|/d^{\star} measures the deviation from the desired local depth d⋆d^{\star}, and Δb=Var⁡({bi}i∈𝒯v)/(b⋆)2\Delta_{b}=\mathrm{Var}(\{b_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{v}})/(b^{\star})^{2} measures the imbalance of the branching distribution with respect to the desired branching factor b⋆b^{\star}. This score is high when the subtree has a reasonable depth and a stable branching pattern, and decreases when the subtree becomes overly shallow, overly deep, or structurally imbalanced.

Red\mathrm{Red} measures redundancy among sibling nodes. We estimate it using pairwise semantic similarity between sibling intents and their attached evidence, with an LLM redundancy judgment for near-duplicate subtopics when similarity alone is ambiguous.

Generation utility. Generation utility evaluates whether the updated local scaffold can support grounded writing:

Ugen=α​ρsup+β​ρcov−γ​ρred.U_{\text{gen}}=\alpha\rho_{\text{sup}}+\beta\rho_{\text{cov}}-\gamma\rho_{\text{red}}. (19)

The Reporter Agent first performs local trial writing on the affected node or subtree. We then score the generated draft from three aspects. ρsup\rho_{\text{sup}} measures factual support. We split the trial draft into claim units and use an NLI model to estimate whether each claim is entailed by the evidence attached to the target node:

ρsup=1|𝒞|​∑c∈𝒞maxe∈ℰv⁡pNLI​(entail∣e,c),\rho_{\text{sup}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\max_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{v}}p_{\text{NLI}}(\mathrm{entail}\mid e,c), (20)

where 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the set of claims extracted from the trial draft. ρcov\rho_{\text{cov}} measures intent coverage. We ask an LLM judge to compare the node intent with the generated local draft and return a normalized score indicating whether the draft covers the required aspects. ρred\rho_{\text{red}} penalizes repeated content in the trial draft and semantic overlap with neighboring sections, estimated by semantic similarity and an LLM redundancy check.

Appendix B Experiment Datasets

We evaluate our approach on two widely used benchmarks targeting end-to-end deep research agent evaluation. Key statistics are summarized in Table 7.

❶DeepResearch Bench Du et al. (2025).

A benchmark of 100 PhD level tasks (50 EN and 50 ZH) across 22 expert curated domains, with the topical distribution calibrated against 96,147 real world user queries. Evaluation combines RACE, an LLM judge protocol that scores reports against a reference along adaptively weighted dimensions (comprehensiveness, insight, instruction following, readability), and FACT, which verifies citation and claim pairs to report citation accuracy (C. Acc.) and effective citations per task (E. Cit.).

❷DeepResearch Gym Coelho et al. (2025).

An open-source sandbox built on top of the Researchy Questions dataset. Following the released pipeline, we run our system on a 100-query subset sampled by document-click frequency, where higher-clicked queries naturally elicit multi-source exploration and long-form synthesis. Each report is then scored under an LLM-as-a-judge protocol along six complementary dimensions: Clarity, Depth, Balance, Breadth, Support and Insightfulness.

❸Multi-Turn Refinement Extension.

To evaluate follow-up interaction, we construct a multi-turn extension based on DeepResearch Bench. For each sampled first-turn query qq and its corresponding report yy, we generate follow-up instructions q′q^{\prime} that cover common ways users refine a deep research report: asking for deeper explanation of a local point, requesting additional evidence or citations, adding a new comparison target or constraint, adjusting the presentation, or correcting an erroneous definition or premise. This yields triples (q,y,q′)(q,y,q^{\prime}) that test whether an agent can revise an existing report without unnecessarily changing unaffected content. We evaluate the updated reports with an LLM judge on five 0–20 dimensions: Ins. for follow-up instruction satisfaction, Evi. for evidence support of new or modified claims, Log. for consistency with the surviving report, Com. for preserving important first-turn content while completing the follow-up, and Exp. for clarity and rigor of expression. Tot. is the sum of the five scores.

Appendix C Baseline Implementation Details

We compare our method against baselines drawn from three paradigms (Naive, Single-Agent, and Multi-Agent), covering distinct strategies for reasoning, retrieval, and agent coordination. Implementation details for each paradigm are described below.

❶Naive.

Naive baselines do not involve explicit agentic reasoning or coordination mechanisms. They either rely solely on the LLM’s parametric knowledge or incorporate retrieval in a fixed, heuristic manner.

  • •

    Prompt. A non-retrieval baseline where the LLM directly generates the final report from the input query using only its parametric knowledge, without any external evidence.

  • •

    RAG. A retrieval-augmented baseline that issues the input query to the search API once, concatenates the top-ranked passages with the query, and prompts the LLM to produce the report in a single pass.

❷Single-Agent.

Single-Agent baselines rely on a single LLM that alternates between reasoning and tool use through prompting, without explicit coordination among multiple agents.

  • •

    ReAct Yao et al. (2022a). ReAct interleaves reasoning and tool invocation in a single loop, enabling the model to iteratively retrieve information and update its reasoning before producing the final answer.

  • •

    IRCoT Trivedi et al. (2023). IRCoT alternates retrieval and chain-of-thought reasoning, using intermediate reasoning steps to formulate new retrieval queries and progressively accumulate evidence.

  • •

    WebShaper Tao et al. (2025). WebShaper formulates information seeking as an iterative query expansion and refinement process, gradually constructing a structured evidence set for answer synthesis. We directly report the WebShaper results published on the WebWeaver benchmark for comparison.

❸Multi-Agent.

Multi-Agent baselines decompose the task into multiple interacting agents, leveraging either centralized coordination or automated agent orchestration strategies.

  • •

    STORM Shao et al. (2024a). STORM generates long-form, Wikipedia-style reports through a multi-perspective pipeline that first asks specialized agents to brainstorm an outline from different viewpoints, then conducts grounded conversations to gather evidence, and finally writes the article section by section. Based on their open-source implementation, we conducted experiments adapting the ’bocha’ search engine as the retrieval module.

  • •

    WebWeaver Li et al. (2025). WebWeaver employs a planner agent and a writer agent that collaborate over a dynamically evolving outline and an evidence memory bank: the planner interleaves search and outline updates, while the writer composes each section by retrieving only the locally relevant evidence to mitigate long-context drift. Building upon their open-source implementation, we integrated the Bocha search engine and conducted experiments.

  • •

    EDR Prabhakar et al. (2025). EDR (Enterprise Deep Research) is a steerable, multi-agent system that coordinates specialized domain agents (e.g., Master Planner, Academic/GitHub/LinkedIn Searchers) and enterprise tools (e.g., NL2SQL). It produces comprehensive research reports through iterative refinement, explicit citation tracking, and a reflection mechanism to address knowledge gaps. In our experiments, we built upon the open-source EDR framework and integrated the Bocha search engine to ensure a fair comparison.

  • •

    StackPlanner Zhang et al. (2026). StackPlanner adopts a stack-based planning controller that pushes and pops sub-goals during exploration, allowing the agent to recursively decompose the research task, dispatch sub-queries to retrieval tools, and assemble the final report from the resolved sub-goals.

Appendix D Implementation Details

We implement ScaffoldAgent without any additional fine-tuning. All LLM interactions are performed through API calls, using Qwen3-32B or DeepSeek for both outline planning and report generation. We adopt BoCha as the default web search backend, retrieving five documents during initialization and eight documents for each subsequent expansion or update query. The outline optimization process is terminated after 20 iterations.

All retrieved documents are encoded using text-embedding-3-small. The resulting 1,536-dimensional embeddings are used to compute all similarity-based metrics, including relevance, novelty, memory retrieval, and sibling-cohesion scores via cosine similarity. We do not use a local encoder for embedding-based retrieval. Instead, local models are reserved for citation verification. Specifically, the system first employs a sentence-transformers CrossEncoder based on nli-deberta-v3-small; when unavailable, DeepSeek is used as a fallback natural language inference (NLI) verifier.

For all experiments, we set λ1=λ2=λ3=1/3\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=\lambda_{3}=1/3. Within the utility formulation, we use wrel=0.6w_{\mathrm{rel}}=0.6 and wnov=0.4w_{\mathrm{nov}}=0.4 for retrieval, wcoh=0.4w_{\mathrm{coh}}=0.4, wbal=0.2w_{\mathrm{bal}}=0.2, and wred=0.4w_{\mathrm{red}}=0.4 for structural optimization, and α=0.4\alpha=0.4, β=0.4\beta=0.4, and γ=0.2\gamma=0.2 for generation.

Appendix E Additional Experiments

❶Inference-Cost Comparison. Beyond quality, we also report inference cost as a standalone efficiency check. Table 9 shows the average per-query inference cost. ScaffoldAgent consumes 26.3k tokens, issues 8.2 search calls, and finishes in 116.7 s, using 29% fewer tokens and 49% fewer search calls than WebWeaver (37.2k / 15.9), and running 4.3×\times faster than EDR (500.5 s) at comparable token cost. The utility-guided action selection concentrates retrieval on high-utility nodes, so the RACE and FACT gains in Sections ❶ and ❷ do not come at the price of runaway inference cost.

❷Outline Tree Statistics.

Figure 4 compares the outline structures produced by different methods. ScaffoldAgent yields the deepest trees (3.09) while keeping the node count moderate (16.38), close to StackPlanner (16.67) and well below EDR (22.07), suggesting that Contraction controls tree growth. More importantly, ScaffoldAgent achieves the highest evidence density, with 5.85 documents per node versus 3.59 for EDR, 2.18 for StackPlanner, and 2.02 for WebWeaver. Thus, ScaffoldAgent does not simply expand the outline; it builds a compact scaffold with richer evidence support for each section.

❸Report Length Distribution

Figure 5 compares the distribution of generated report lengths across methods. Naive and single-agent methods mostly produce short reports below 4K characters, whereas multi-agent methods show substantially longer outputs. Among them, ScaffoldAgent has the highest median length, around 22K characters, and a relatively compact interquartile range compared with STORM, whose outputs vary widely from short reports to over 30K characters. EDR is more concentrated around 6–9K characters, and WebWeaver remains close to the short-report regime. These patterns suggest that ScaffoldAgent’s optimized outline scaffold supports more extensive and stable synthesis, while the main quality metrics confirm that the longer outputs are accompanied by stronger depth, breadth, and grounding.

Appendix F Computational Resources and Software Environment

Experiments were conducted using API-based inference. The Qwen-series backbone was deployed on a single-machine multi-GPU server equipped with 2 NVIDIA A800 GPUs with 80GB memory each, dual Intel Xeon Platinum 8358 CPUs with 64 physical cores and 128 threads in total, and 1024GB of DDR4 memory. The server ran Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS with Docker, and the inference service was built with vLLM 0.13.0 under FP16 precision. The software environment used Python 3.13.12 and HuggingFace Transformers 4.57.3. On the client side, our agent framework was implemented with Python 3.11, LiteLLM 1.63.11, OpenAI 2.8.1, MCP 1.6.0, LangChain 0.3.25, and LangGraph 0.4.10 for API calls, tool interaction, and agent orchestration.

Appendix G The Use of Large Language Models

In this work, Large Language Models (LLMs) were used for language polishing, figure design assistance, and coding support. Specifically, LLMs were used to refine the clarity, grammar, and readability of the manuscript, improve stylistic quality, and suggest alternative phrasings to reduce redundant or repetitive expressions. LLMs were also used to provide inspiration for figure design, visualization layouts, and graphical presentation, with final figures created and curated by the authors. In addition, LLMs assisted with code development by suggesting code snippets and troubleshooting strategies. All content generated by LLMs was carefully reviewed, verified, and revised by the authors before inclusion. The research design, methodology, critical analyses, and all final decisions were independently conducted by the authors. LLMs were not involved in generating the core research ideas, scientific contributions, or conclusions of this work.
